subject: Archaeology
title: Domesticating Animals: Wolves to Dogs
description: A micro-lesson that makes Domesticating Animals: Wolves to Dogs usable.

hook.text: Dogs were the first domesticated animal — tamed from wolves at least 15,000 years ago, long before farming began.

buildup.text: Wolves that tolerated humans scavenged from campsites. Over generations, the friendliest ones were kept and bred.

discovery.text: A 14,000-year-old burial in Germany contains a puppy placed beside a human. The bond was already deep.

twist.text: Domestication changed wolf anatomy: skulls shortened, teeth shrank, and floppy ears appeared — the 'domestication syndrome.'

climax.text: Dogs helped humans hunt, herd, and guard. Some researchers argue we could not have built civilization without them.

punchline.text: We think we tamed wolves. They may have tamed us first.

quiz.question: What physical changes occurred in wolves during domestication?
options: They became larger and more aggressive
Skulls shortened, teeth shrank, and floppy ears appeared
Their fur became waterproof and their legs grew longer

details.summary: Dogs were the first domesticated animal, diverging from wolves at least 15,000 years ago. The process likely involved wolves self-selecting by scavenging near human camps, with the tamest individuals gradually integrated into human society for hunting, guarding, and companionship.
details.whyItMatters: Dog domestication shows how human-animal relationships can transform both species. It was the first step in a process that led to domestication of livestock, fundamentally changing human subsistence and society.
takeaways: Dogs diverged from wolves at least 15,000 years ago
Self-domestication by scavenging wolves was likely the first step
Dogs were the first domesticated animal, preceding agriculture

faq.question: Did humans deliberately domesticate wolves?
faq.answer: Probably not at first. The most accepted theory is that tolerant wolves scavenged near human camps, and the tamest ones were gradually accepted. Over generations, these proto-dogs became increasingly dependent on and cooperative with humans through mutual benefit.

faq.question: Where were dogs first domesticated?
faq.answer: The location is debated. Genetic evidence has pointed to Europe, Central Asia, East Asia, and the Middle East at various times. Dogs may have been domesticated independently in more than one region, making a single origin point difficult to identify.
